source_text: Vita autem, in qua regnaturi sunt sancti, aeterna monstratur; ergo et mors, quae iniquitatem voluntariam sequitur, aeterna credatur. Itaque sicut per unius delictum in omnes homines in condemnationem, sic et per unius iustitiam in omnes homines in iustificationem vitae. Sicut enim per unius inoboedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita et per unius oboedientiam iusti constituentur multi [n347] . Omnis est soluta perplexitas, impudenter de universitate calumnia concitatur, ineptissime in scirpo nodus quaeritur. Pronuntiat Apostolus non omnes esse, sed multos, qui per inoboedientiam primi hominis peccata didicissent, et multos esse, non omnes, qui per alterius oboedientiam iustitiam essent adepti. Nihil hic de exortu humanitatis agitur, mores in diversis studiis publicantur; inoboedientia et oboedientia studiorum operam, non generationis ostendit. Certe ubi opportunius, si quid secundum te saperet Apostolus, pronuntiaret omnes ad condemnationem ire nascendo, paucos autem ad vitam credendo quam in hoc loco, ubi summa disputationis complenda erat? Debuit enim dicere: Sicut per inoboedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt omnes, immo non per inoboedientiam, sed sicut per generationem primi hominis peccatores nati sunt omnes, ita et per unius oboedientiam iusti constituentur multi.
pass_a_gloss: But the life in which the holy are about to reign is shown eternal; therefore also death, which follows a voluntary iniquity, let it be believed eternal. Therefore as through the offense of one into all human beings into condemnation, so also through the justice of one into all human beings into justification of life. For as through the disobedience of one many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one many will be constituted just. Every perplexity has been loosed, a calumny is shamelessly stirred about universality, a knot is most ineptly sought in a bulrush. The Apostle pronounces that they are not all, but many, who had learned sins through the disobedience of the first human being, and that they are many, not all, who through the obedience of another had obtained justice. Nothing here is acted about the rising of humanity, manners are published in diverse pursuits; disobedience and obedience show a work of pursuits, not of generation. Certainly where more opportunely, if the Apostle tasted anything according to you, would he pronounce that all go unto condemnation by being born, but few unto life by believing, than in this place, where the sum of the disputation was to be completed? For he ought to have said: As through the disobedience of one human being all were constituted sinners, nay not through disobedience, but as through the generation of the first human being all were born sinners, so also through the obedience of one many will be constituted just.

lemmas.lexica: LS generatio; Blaise vs imitatio in Rom 5:12
LS delictum; Blaise Rom 5 delictum vs donum
LS iustificatio; Blaise forensic making-just, not later system
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: The life in which the holy will reign is shown to be eternal. Therefore the death that follows voluntary wickedness should also be understood as eternal. ‘Therefore, as through one man’s offense it came upon all human beings to condemnation, so through one man’s righteousness it came upon all human beings to justification of life. For just as through one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous’ (Romans 5:18–19). Every difficulty is resolved. It is shameless to stir up a false accusation about universality; it is utterly foolish to hunt for a knot in a smooth rush. The apostle declares that not all but many learned sins through the first man’s disobedience, and that many, not all, obtained righteousness through the other’s obedience. Human origin is not under discussion here. Conduct is displayed in opposing pursuits. Disobedience and obedience show the activity of deliberate conduct, not of generation. Surely, if the apostle thought as you do, where could he more fittingly have declared that all go to condemnation by birth but few to life by believing, than here, where the argument’s conclusion was to be completed? He ought to have said: ‘Just as through one man’s disobedience all were made sinners’—or rather, not ‘through disobedience,’ but ‘Just as through the first man’s generation all were born sinners, so through one man’s obedience many will be made righteous.’
